title: Big O Notation
definition: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as its input gets larger, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
explanation:
Imagine counting the basic steps an algorithm takes for an input of size *n*. A loop that touches each item once takes about *n* steps; a loop nested inside another takes about *n×n*. Big O keeps only the part that dominates as *n* grows: 3n + 10 becomes O(n), and n² + 100n becomes O(n²).

The common classes, from slowest-growing to fastest-growing, are O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) linearithmic, O(n²) quadratic and O(2ⁿ) exponential. Doubling the input roughly doubles the work for O(n), quadruples it for O(n²), and adds only one extra step for O(log n).

Big O describes *growth*, not speed. An O(n) algorithm with a large constant can lose to an O(n²) one on small inputs. Strictly, O(...) is an upper bound; in everyday use people quote it for the worst case, and sometimes loosely for the typical case. The same notation applies to memory, which is why you will often see time and space complexity discussed together.
whyItMatters: It lets you compare approaches before writing any code and predict how a program will behave when the data grows from a thousand items to a billion. Most performance problems in practice come from choosing an algorithm whose growth rate does not fit the data.
